etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English hevy, heviȝ, from Old English hefiġ, hefeġ, hæfiġ (“heavy; important, grave, severe, serious; oppressive, grievous; slow, dull”), from Proto-West Germanic *habīg (“heavy, hefty, weighty”), from Proto-Germanic *habīgaz (“heavy, hefty, weighty”), from Proto-Indo-European *keh₂p- (“to take, grasp, hold”).

definitions.definition: (of a physical object) Having great weight.

quote.citation: 1897 December (indicated as 1898), Winston Churchill, chapter II, in The Celebrity: An Episode, New York, N.Y.: The Macmillan Company; London: Macmillan & Co., Ltd., →OCLC:
quote.text: Sunning himself on the board steps, I saw for the first time Mr. Farquhar Fenelon Cooke. […] A silver snaffle on a heavy leather watch guard which connected the pockets of his corduroy waistcoat, together with a huge gold stirrup in his Ascot tie, sufficiently proclaimed his tastes.

quote.citation: 2002, Eva Brann, Homeric Moments, page 48:
quote.text: But now, ten years later, after his recent shipwreck, he cannot compete as a runner, though he can outthrow the slighter Phaeacians with the heaviest discus.

quote.citation: 2015 May 18, Angus Chen, How We Store Food At Home Could Be Linked To How Much We Eat:
quote.text: In other research, scientists have found that people who kept cereal out in the open were often about 20 pounds heavier than people who kept cereal behind closed doors.

definitions.definition: (of a topic) Serious, somber.
Not easy to bear; burdensome; oppressive.

quote.text: Sent hither by my Husband to impart the heavy news.

definitions.definition: (British, slang, dated) Good.
(dated, late 1960s, 1970s, US) Profound.

quote.text: The ovarian response to gonadotropic hormones may be erratic at first, so that irregular or heavy bleeding sometimes occurs

definitions.definition: (slang) Armed.
(of music) Loud, distorted, or intense.
(of weather) Hot and humid.
(of a person) Doing the specified activity more intensely than most other people.

quote.text: He was described in the theatrical prints as the “veteran Blenkinsop”—“the useful Blenkinsop”—“that old favourite of the public, Blenkinsop”—those parts in the drama, which are called the heavy fathers, were usually assigned to this veteran, who, indeed, acted the heavy father in public, as in private life.

definitions.definition: (of the eyes) With eyelids difficult to keep open due to tiredness.

quote.citation: 2021 December, The Road Ahead, Brisbane, page 11, column 3:
quote.text: Watch for the signs of fatigue, including yawning, blinking and heavy eyes.

definitions.definition: (of food) High in fat or protein; difficult to digest.

When the national grid suffers its next huge outage, as it did in July 2012 when hundreds of millions were left in the dark, look for specks of light in the villages.

definitions.definition: Laden with that which is weighty; encumbered; burdened; bowed down, either with an actual burden, or with grief, pain, disappointment, etc.

definitions.definition: Not raised or leavened.
(of wines or spirits) Having much body or strength.
(obsolete) With child; pregnant.
(physics) Containing one or more isotopes that are heavier than the normal one.
(petroleum) Having high viscosity.
(finance) Of a market: in which the price of shares is declining.

definitions.definition: (nautical, military) Heavily-armed.

definitions.definition: (aviation, of an aircraft) Having a relatively high takeoff weight and payload.

definitions.definition: (India, colloquial) very
